title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Fabrication | Dye PT (US)
description: On-site liquid penetrant testing for US fabricators: stainless, aluminum and nickel alloy welds, repairs and attachments to ASME and AWS. Request a PT quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Fabrication and Welding in the United States
html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT, also called dye penetrant inspection) shows cracks, laps, porosity and other surface-breaking flaws on welds and fabricated parts of any non-porous material, including the stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys that magnetic particle methods cannot examine. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to fabrication shops and yards across the United States to examine welds and machined surfaces to ASME and AWS requirements and report every indication. To start, request a PT inspection quote.

Where penetrant testing earns its place in a fabrication scope

Fabrication shops that work in stainless steel, duplex, aluminum and nickel alloys depend on penetrant testing more than shops that build carbon steel only. Austenitic stainless steel vessels, process piping for chemical and food service, aluminum structures and heat exchanger components cannot be magnetized, so the choice for a surface examination is penetrant. Even on carbon steel, PT is used where magnetizing is awkward or where the specification asks for it on a root pass, a seal weld or a weld overlay.

The principle is simple: a low-viscosity liquid is drawn by capillary action into any flaw open to the surface, excess is removed, and a developer draws the trapped liquid back out so the flaw shows as a visible mark. That simplicity is also why the method is easy to do badly. Contamination, rough surfaces and poor dwell control hide real flaws as readily as they create false ones.

The fabrication jobs we examine

  • Stainless and nickel alloy vessels and piping: final welds, root passes where the code or owner calls for an in-process examination, weld overlay and nozzle attachment welds.
  • Aluminum and duplex fabrications: structural and pressure-boundary welds in material that has no magnetic response.
  • Repair areas: excavations where a crack was ground out, re-examined before re-welding, and the finished repair examined again.
  • Tank components: nozzle necks, manway frames and attachment welds on API 650 tanks, where penetrant is chosen for stainless or for areas where particles cannot be applied.
  • Machined and cast fittings: sealing faces, threaded connections and nozzle forgings that an owner wants checked at receiving.

The weld-specific page, dye penetrant weld inspection, covers the technique stage by stage.

Codes and acceptance

Penetrant testing in fabrication is governed by the same family of codes as the other methods. ASME Section V Article 6 provides the examination requirements; ASTM E165 is the standard practice for penetrant examination of general industrial parts; and the acceptance criteria come from the construction code: ASME Section VIII for vessels, ASME B31.3 for piping, AWS D1.1 where the structural code allows penetrant as an alternative, and API 650 for tanks. Our guide to ASME Section V Article 6 explains what the article sets down.

The technician does not decide acceptance. We measure each indication, classify it as linear or rounded according to the code, report its location and dimensions, and state which acceptance criteria the report applies. The owner, the fabricator's quality manager or the third party named in the contract makes the accept or reject decision.

Technique details that control the result

The steps in a penetrant examination are fixed by the procedure, and the times and temperatures are not suggestions.

  • Surface preparation: the surface is cleaned of oil, grease, scale and weld spatter. Grinding or blasting can smear metal over a flaw and close it, so many specifications call for an etch or a cleaning step after mechanical preparation.
  • Penetrant type and removal: visible dye with solvent removal is typical in shop and field work; fluorescent systems are used where the specification wants more sensitivity and a darkened area is available. Water-washable systems suit rougher surfaces but need controlled washing.
  • Temperature: the standard ASME Section V Article 6 range is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. A job that falls outside the range needs a procedure demonstrated at the real working temperature, which matters for outdoor yards in winter and for welds that are still warm.
  • Dwell and developer: penetrant dwell and developer time are set by the material and the flaw type being sought. Developer is applied thin and evenly; a heavy coat can hide a fine crack.
  • Contaminant control on stainless and nickel alloys: penetrant materials used on austenitic stainless and nickel-base alloys are controlled for halogen and sulfur content, and the procedure records the batch. This is a quality-record item that owners of stainless equipment check.
  • Interpretation: indications are evaluated within the time window the procedure gives, in adequate white light or ultraviolet light, and the area is cleaned after examination.

What PT finds in fabricated welds, and what it misses

PT is a good fit for cracks, cold laps, surface porosity and incomplete fusion at the surface of any non-porous material. It will not find flaws that are not open to the surface: subsurface porosity, slag inside the weld, lack of fusion buried in a groove joint. A smeared, peened or coated surface can seal a surface flaw so that penetrant cannot enter it, which is why surface condition goes on the report.

Method selection is part of our scope review. On ferromagnetic carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in fabrication is usually faster and also finds shallow subsurface flaws. For through-thickness flaws in groove welds, ultrasonic testing in fabrication is the method that reaches the volume of the joint. The related guide, MT versus PT, compares the two surface methods in plain terms.

What the PT report contains

Typical contents of a fabrication PT report
ItemWhat we record
Part and weldJob, drawing, weld number, material, thickness and surface condition at examination
ProcedureWritten procedure and revision, code edition, acceptance standard
MaterialsPenetrant, remover and developer by manufacturer and batch, and whether the family is visible or fluorescent
Process controlPart temperature, penetrant dwell time, developer time and the pre-cleaning method
PersonnelTechnician and level under the written practice, with the Level III who approved the procedure
FindingsLocation, length and type of each indication, accept or reject and a sketch or photograph of repaired areas

Overlay, seal welds and repair excavations

Three situations produce more penetrant work in a fabrication shop than any others. Weld overlay, where a corrosion-resistant alloy is deposited on a carbon steel surface, is examined to confirm there are no cracks or lack of bond showing at the surface of the finished layer and at the edges of the cladding. Seal welds on threaded connections, which are not structural but must hold a fluid, are examined because a pinhole in a seal weld is a leak path. Repair excavations are examined twice: once after the defect has been ground out, to prove the flaw is gone before anyone welds, and again after the repair weld is finished and dressed.

Each situation has its own records need. Overlay examinations should identify which layer or pass was examined; seal weld lists should be tied to the line or equipment tag; excavations should be located by weld number and clock position or station so the repair crew and the next inspector can find them. We write the report that way so it can be read by someone who was not on the floor that day, and so a repair history for a vessel can be rebuilt from the file years later.

What to send us for a quote

  • Governing code, edition and acceptance criteria
  • Weld list or drawing marks, quantities and the examination percentage
  • Material grade, whether it is stainless, nickel alloy or aluminum, and thickness
  • Any customer limit on halogen, sulfur or chloride content in the penetrant materials
  • Surface condition, how it was prepared, and weld stage
  • Whether a fluorescent method is specified and whether the area can be darkened
  • Working temperature range at the site, witness points and the shop address with badging details

Planning notes for the shop

Penetrant examinations are slower per weld than a magnetic particle pass because every step has a dwell. The schedule should allow for cleaning, penetrant application, dwell, removal, developer and interpretation, and for a repeat after repair. In a cold shop or an outdoor yard the temperature window can be the controlling item, and a heated enclosure or a qualified low-temperature procedure may be needed. Solvents are flammable, so the shop's hot-work rules and ventilation requirements apply while the crew is working.

Hold points matter in stainless fabrication because passivation, pickling and final cleaning often follow the examination. If PT has to come first, plan to clean thoroughly afterward; if the specification forbids chloride-bearing materials, tell us before the crew travels to your site. Procedure work, including a written procedure reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III, is available through NDT technical procedure development.

Training your quality staff

If you would rather run penetrant testing in-house, PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training cover the theory, and the penetrant testing simulator gives your people repetition before they touch production work. The employer issues the personnel qualification under its written practice. For the manufacturing sector overall, see NDT training for manufacturing.

Limits of this service

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and the specialist techniques we leave out are not offered on this page. We do not weld, grind, pickle or passivate, and we do not choose the examination percentage; the code and the contract do. Penetrant finds only flaws open to the surface; for buried flaws the scope must add ultrasonic testing. More background is in the national penetrant testing overview and the weld inspection page.

faq.q: Can PT be used on stainless steel pressure vessels?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant is the usual surface method for austenitic stainless steel because it cannot be magnetized. Many owners also set limits on halogen and sulfur content in the penetrant materials, and we record the batches used in the report.

faq.q: What temperature range does penetrant testing allow?
faq.a: The standard range in ASME Section V Article 6 is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Work colder or hotter than that needs a procedure demonstrated for the real conditions. We confirm site conditions with you before the crew travels.

faq.q: When is PT the wrong method?
faq.a: PT cannot find flaws that are not open to the surface, so it is wrong for buried lack of fusion, internal slag or subsurface porosity. It also struggles on rough, coated or smeared surfaces. In those cases ultrasonic testing or a surface preparation change is needed.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects penetrant indications?
faq.a: The code and the party named in the contract decide. We measure and classify each indication and report which criterion was used; the owner, its inspector or the fabricator's quality manager makes the accept or reject call.

Only if the specification or procedure says so. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive but needs a darkened area and an ultraviolet light measured at the part. Visible dye with solvent removal is common in the shop and field.

faq.q: Do you examine welds after post-weld heat treatment?
faq.a: Yes. If the code or owner wants an examination after heat treatment, we plan the visit around it and the report states that the examination followed heat treatment, which matters when cracks open during thermal cycling.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote penetrant testing?
faq.a: Send the code and edition, weld list or drawing marks, material and thickness, surface condition, any chemistry limits on penetrant materials, fluorescent or visible requirement, working temperature range, witness points and the shop address.

faq.q: Can you examine weld repairs before and after re-welding?
faq.a: Yes. We examine the excavation before re-welding to confirm the flaw has been removed, then the completed repair. Both examinations are reported against the original weld number so the repair history is easy to follow.

No. Under the SNT-TC-1A system the employer sets the written practice and issues the qualification. Our Level II technicians perform and interpret examinations, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report.
